scores.name: LIT-80: 80 live sessions x 50 turns, recorded gaps x60 capped at 600 s, cohort start ramped at 1 session/s
scores.comment: I re-ran the exact recipe in the queue-aware model (tiersim.py, calibrated on the x70 campaign). The tiered arms are stable: about 7 in flight, queue 0, mean TTFT 0.42 s. The SSD serves 6.4% of returns (251). The proposal's own unqueued model says about 9%, and the queue-aware model counted a third fewer SSD returns than were measured at x70, so 6-10% is the plausible range. hbm_host collapses in the second half (model: queue about 60, mean TTFT about 1 min; this model overstates collapsed arms by 1.35-2x) and hbm_lru collapses throughout. That repeats the x70 pattern. Two numbers are overstated. The stated working set of 3.11M assumes all 80 sessions reach turn 50 together; because they drift apart, the live peak is about 2.1M (1.3x L2) and stays above L2 for about 22 min. The worry about in-flight requests filling L1 is also too strong: the model shows about 7 in flight, not 14. Realism is the weak point. Multiplying every gap by 60 makes each one about 40 s, while every measured source has a sub-second median and only rare long pauses. AgentX forbids re-timing recorded gaps, and no verified source stretches them. The mean matches the idle time per LLM call derived from TraceLab; the shape does not. Its strength is that it needs no code change and joins the existing x70/x10/x1 series. It is best kept as the idle-dominated upper bound.

scores.name: c72-t50-ln40: 72 live sessions × 50 turns, lognormal gaps with a 40 s median, Poisson ramp at 0.5 sessions/s
scores.comment: The re-simulation reproduces the proposal's own numbers. Tiered arms: queue 0, mean TTFT 0.33 s, SSD on 7.6% of returns (268), working set peaking at 2.06M and above L2 for about 22 min. hbm_host (queue about 47, TTFT about 49 s) and hbm_lru (about 115 s) collapse late, as in LIT-80. The gap law is a single lognormal with median 40 s and sigma 0.8. It has no sub-second tool gaps and no heavy human-think tail, and its parameters were tuned with Little's law to hit a target load. It matches neither this trace nor TraceLab or MORI. It breaks comparability with both the trace and the gap-scale series, and its idle-to-active ratio (about 10) is twice TraceLab's R. The baked-gap plumbing is correct: it avoids --gap-sample. But in a paper this is the hardest of the three to defend, and it offers nothing over LIT-80 except a lighter early peak (1.2 vs 1.95 turns/s).

scores.name: C80 x 50 turns, TraceLab tool+think gaps (smallest load that reaches the SSD)
scores.comment: This proposal has the best-anchored gap law: TraceLab tool latency plus a human pause with p = 1/8.8. It uses the closed loop with replacement that AgentX and MORI use, and C=80 equals MORI's top concurrency on an H200 running Qwen3-30B-A3B. Re-simulated in the queue-aware model across 3 seeds and 2 stress variants, the tiered and hbm_host arms are stable (queue about 0, mean TTFT 0.19 vs 0.43 s). The SSD serves 2.2-2.7% of returns (about 190-220), and almost all of them follow gaps of 10 min or more, which is exactly TraceLab's miss pattern. The unqueued stack-distance model gives the same L1/L2/L3 split of 0.90/0.08/0.025. Two corrections. (1) hbm_lru is not in 'mild overload': with about 30% of returns recomputing it collapses like x10/x1 (about 0.33 turns/s, TTFT 1-2 min). (2) With only the 228 conversations of exactly 50 turns, the pool runs dry at about 110 min at about 1.45 turns/s. The pool of 283 conversations with at least 45 turns fixes that. The weak point is tier relevance: timeout and wait_complete will come out equal, and hbm_host and the three-tier arms look alike in aggregate, so the SSD result has to be shown per gap class.

recommended.name: RT-80: TraceLab cadence, 80 live sessions x 45-50 turns, closed loop with replacement
recommended.gap_model:
Gaps are fixed per (conversation, turn >= 1). They are baked into the pre_gap field of a derived trace and replayed with GAP=1 GAP_CAP=0, so all four arms sleep the same gap on the same turn. (The client's --gap-sample would not do this: it draws from one shared RNG in completion order.)
Rule: let r = random.Random((SEED<<32) ^ (i<<12) ^ t), with SEED=1 and i = the conversation's index in the derived list.
- tool = min(216 s, 0.3 s x exp(2.976 z1)). This is TraceLab's Table 7 tool latency: p50 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s, capped at its p99 of 3.6 min. Capped mean 8.5 s.
- With probability 1/8.8, add think = min(1,800 s, 84 s x exp(2.098 z2)). This is TraceLab's human think time: p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min, one pause per 8.8 LLM calls. The 30-min cap leaves 92.8% of pauses unchanged. Capped mean 328 s.
- gap = tool + think, measured from the end of the reply (the client's convention, and TraceLab's).
Result for seed 1 (13,706 gaps): mean 46.5 s, p50 0.48 s, p75 5.6 s, p90 62 s, p95 216 s, p99 1,476 s. 41.6% exceed 1 s, 10.2% exceed 1 min, 3.1% exceed 5 min, 2.0% exceed 10 min and 1.3% exceed 20 min. 11.4% of gaps contain a think pause.
The original gap is kept as pre_gap_orig and the think part as gap_think, for analysis by gap class. Generator: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/mine/make_tl_trace.py. A dry run reproduced these statistics exactly; it has not written the file into the repo.
Why not the trace's own gaps: they come from an unattended SWE-bench harness (p50 0.71 s, p99 11.8 s) with no human pauses, so at any load this box can sustain they never reach L2 or L3.
Why not a uniform scale: no verified source rescales recorded gaps (AgentX forbids it). A uniform x60 matches the literature's mean of about 46 s but not its shape, whose median is 0.5 s.
recommended.arrival_model:
Closed loop with replacement, as in AgentX and MORI. At most 80 sessions are live. A session keeps its slot through its tool and think gaps, and when it finishes the next waiting conversation starts at once.
Start-up: conversations arrive as a seeded Poisson process at 0.1/s (ARRIVAL=0.1, SEED=0). The 80 slots fill in about 13 min and later arrivals wait for a slot. The mix of session ages is steady from about 30 min.
Wall cap: MAX_SECONDS = CLIENT_TIMEOUT = 7,200 s per arm. Analysis window: 30-120 min.
run_compare.sh knobs: TRACE=<derived file> NCONV=283 C=80 TURNS=50 GAP=1 GAP_CAP=0 OFFSET=0 SEED=0 CLIENT_TIMEOUT=7200 ARRIVAL=0.1. All other settings as in campaigns 7-9: MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, CTX=131072, LEVEL=NAT160, bf16 KV, same four arms. ARRIVAL reaches start_client.sh through the environment but is not written to config.txt, so add it by hand. GAP_CAP must be 0: the script's default of 600 would clip the 30-min pauses to 10 min, which lands exactly on the L2/L3 boundary.
recommended.conversation_selection:
Take the 283 conversations with at least 45 turns, in trace order (all SWE-bench, originally minimax-m2.5). Truncate them at 50 turns: the mean is 49.4 turns, 228 have exactly 50, and the total is 13,989 turns. Write them with the baked gaps to a derived trace, for example traces/lmcache_agentic_trace_262k_ge45_tl_s1.json. Set NCONV=283, C=80, TURNS=50, OFFSET=0.
Contexts grow from about 9.9K tokens at turn 1 to 43.6K at the final turn (p50; p10 35.0K, p90 56.9K, max 109K, below CTX 131,072). The mean prompt over a session's life is 28.6K tokens, of which about 21K is private (the 7,808-token system prompt is shared).
In the model, 251 of the 283 conversations start within the 2-hour cap, so the live count stays at 80 and the pool does not run dry. Use the same file and order on all four arms. No conversation is replayed twice, so no cache-busting is needed.
recommended.expected_L3_reach:
About 2.5% of returning turns in the three-tier arms: 2.2-3.3% across seeds and models, or about 190-300 SSD restores per arm in the 30-120 min window. Each restore is about 30K tokens (about 2.9 GB), about 0.5 TB read per arm.
By gap class, from the queue-aware model: gaps under 1 min (91.6% of returns) are served from L1; gaps of 1-5 min (6.9%) from L2; about a quarter of 5-10 min gaps (1.1%) go to the SSD; and essentially all gaps of 10 min or more (2.2%) do.
Why: at about 1.5 turns/s the pools take about 1,070 new tokens/s (515 new input + 213 output per turn), plus re-touches of the roughly 12 active sessions' 25-30K-token contexts. That gives L1 (668K) an effective retention of about 1 min, and L2 (1.63M, a write-through superset of L1) about 6-10 min. The live working set, about 1.7M plus the KV of finished sessions, sits just above L2. So only a return after a gap longer than L2's retention falls to the SSD, which is TraceLab's 'misses start beyond 5 min' pattern. Under TraceLab cadence one call in 8.8 follows a pause, and 17% of pauses exceed 10 min, which gives about 2% of returns.
What each arm pays for those returns: the three-tier arms restore them at about 1.4-1.7 s mean TTFT (p90 about 2.4 s). hbm_host recomputes them at about 4.5-5.2 s (p90 about 8 s). hbm_lru also loses the 1-10 min class and saturates.
The queue-aware model counted a third fewer SSD returns than were measured at x70, so the real share may be about 3-3.5%.
recommended.expected_utilization:
Three-tier arms: about 1.5 turns/s. That is 50-75% of the 2-3 turns/s hit-dominated capacity and about 85% of the 1.77-1.8 turns/s the SSD arms sustained in x70's main window. About 12 requests are in flight, holding about 0.35M tokens of running KV against the 668K L1, so admission is not memory-bound. Prefill takes about 14% of GPU time and the queue is about 0. SSD reads are about 5% busy (restores take about 1.5 s each at the ceiling). L3 write-through is about 0.1-0.13 GB/s (about 6%), or about 0.9 TB per arm, below the 70% cleaner mark.
hbm_host: the same load plus recomputing the about 2.5% of returns that follow long gaps, about 1,000 prefill tok/s or about 20% of the 4,903 tok/s prefill rate. Prefill takes 21-25% of GPU time and the queue stays at 0-0.3. It was stable in 3 of 3 seeds and in both stress variants (ITL x1.3 with L1 x0.9; prefill x0.7).
hbm_lru: demand is about 1.4-1.6x capacity, because every return after more than 1 min (about 9% of returns) recomputes 25-30K tokens. It collapses to about 0.3 turns/s with 35-40 requests waiting and about 2-min TTFT, like x10/x1.
literature_anchors: MORI (UC Berkeley, arXiv 2606.00866): 20/50/80 concurrent programs per replica, including one H200 running Qwen3-30B-A3B (this box's GPU and model). Closed-loop clients sleep the recorded Claude Code tool durations and start a new trace when one finishes; 1-hour runs. C=80 is its top level.

AIPerf InferenceX AgentX MVP (NVIDIA): closed loop with exactly --concurrency live session trees (32 in the quick start, 100 in the narrative). Recorded gaps are replayed end to start; per-trace and per-turn caps or compression are forbidden; only a global 10 s idle guard; 15-30 min runs.
sammshen/agentic-dataset, the converter and run guide for this exact trace: --concurrency 20 live sessions, with the recorded pre_gap as the delay.
SGLang HiCache blog (LMSYS): its multi-turn benchmark example uses 80 clients x 10 rounds. LMCache SageMaker HyperPod blog: 100 users at 8 QPS. AIPerf user-centric tutorial: 15 users at 1 req/s.

TraceLab (UW, arXiv 2606.30560; 4,265 Claude Code/Codex sessions): tool latency p50 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s, p99 3.6 min, mean 18.4 s. Human think time p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min, mean 46.7 min; 8.8 LLM calls per user request; humans idle 92.3% of wall-clock. Prefix hit rate 85.4% at a 1-min TTL, about 94% at 5 min, 98.6% at 1 h; misses start at gaps over 5 min. This is the source of the gap law and of the gap-class analysis.
HF datasets-server statistics for sammshen/lmcache-agentic-traces: pre_gap median 0.706 s, mean 2.02 s, max 1,511 s. The trace's own harness gaps are tool-only.

AA-AgentPerf (Artificial Analysis): closed-loop simulated agents on real OpenCode trajectories (ISL mean about 27K). Tool delays range from under 0.1 s to 5 s with a median of about 1 s; steady phases last at least 10 min; the agent count is found by binary search against SLOs.

LMCache MI300X blog (kv-cache-tester): real-time think-only timing (time-scale 1.0, max-delay 600 s), 4-32 users. The CPU tier pays off only once the sustained working set exceeds HBM, which is why W is sized against L2 here.
Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230, VLDB): SWE-bench agent programs average 10.9 turns with tool time 0.93 ± 3.55 s; Poisson program arrivals of 0.02-0.13/s on one GPU.
recommended.arithmetic:
0) Why not the literature default. C=20-32 at recorded gaps (x1) keeps the live working set at 0.5-0.8M tokens, inside L1 or just above it. In the queue-aware model 99.4% of tokens come from L1, all four arms coincide and L3 is never reached. C=20 gives 1.8 turns/s; C=32 gives 2.1-2.3 turns/s with a queue of about 3, which is at capacity. The SSD can matter only when sessions idle long enough for the working set to exceed L2 at a load the box can sustain, and the only long gaps in the literature are human pauses.
1) Mean gap G. Tool part: lognormal, median 0.3 s, sigma = ln(13.6/0.3)/1.2816 = 2.98, capped at 216 s, capped mean 8.5 s. Think part, with p = 1/8.8 = 0.114: lognormal, median 84 s, sigma = ln(1236/84)/1.2816 = 2.10, capped at 1,800 s (7.2% of pauses capped), capped mean 328 s. E[G] = 8.5 + 0.114 x 328 = 45.8 s; baked seeds give 44.7-48.2 s. p50 0.48 s, p90 62 s, p99 about 1,480 s.
2) Service time per turn S. About 0.2-0.3 s TTFT, plus about 0.1 s to prefill 515 new tokens, plus 213 output tokens at about 31-35 ms ITL with about 12 in flight: about 7-9 s. The models give 8.0-9.3 s.
3) Throughput X = C/(G+S) = 80/(46+8.5) ≈ 1.47 turns/s. The queue-aware model gives 1.47-1.55 in the 30-120 min window across 3 seeds; the stack-distance model gives 1.33-1.52.
4) In flight N = X·S ≈ 1.47 x 8 ≈ 12 (models: 11.8-13.7). Running KV ≈ 12 x 28.6K ≈ 0.34M, below the 0.67M L1.
5) Working set. A session's mean prompt over its life is 28.6K, about 21.0K private. W_live = 7.8K + 80 x 21.0K = 1.69M, about 1.04x L2 and 2.5x L1. The models give a time average of 1.65-1.72M and a peak of 1.8-1.95M. Finished sessions' KV (replaced at about 2.2 sessions/min) adds LRU pressure on top.
6) Retention. New KV ≈ X x (515+213) ≈ 1,070 tok/s ≈ 64K/min, plus re-touches of active contexts. That gives L1 about 1 min and L2 about 6-10 min of effective retention. By gap class in the queue-aware model: under 1 min, 91.6% of returns, served from L1 (TTFT 0.15 s); 1-5 min, 6.9%, from L2; 5-10 min, 1.1%, of which 23% go to the SSD; 10 min or more, 2.2%, all SSD (1.4-1.7 s mean) in the three-tier arms or all recompute in hbm_host (4.5-5.2 s mean, p90 about 8 s).
7) SSD. About 0.035 restores/s x about 30K tokens x 98,304 B ≈ 2.9 GB each, about 1.5 s at 1.88 GiB/s, so the disk is about 5% busy for reads. Write-through is about 0.1-0.13 GB/s. The timeout policy's budget is far above 1.5 s, so timeout and wait_complete should behave the same.
8) Baselines. hbm_host recomputes about 0.035/s x 28K ≈ 1,000 tok/s, about 20% of prefill capacity, so it stays stable (queue 0-0.3). hbm_lru recomputes every return after more than 1 min (about 9%): about 0.13/s x 28K ≈ 3.7K tok/s, about 75% of prefill, plus the queue-time invalidation that follows. It collapses to 0.31-0.34 turns/s with TTFT of about 2 min.
9) Duration. The ramp (80/0.1) takes about 13 min and the run is steady from about 30 min. 283 conversations x 49.4 turns = 13,989 turns, of which 251 conversations start within 2 h, so the pool does not run dry. The 7,200 s cap gives about 7,900-8,400 turns in the 30-120 min window for a healthy arm. Four arms x (2 h + about 10 min for boot and L3 wipe) ≈ 8.7 h.
10) Against x70. 37.5% fewer sessions (80 vs 128), 25% more turns (50 vs 40), a similar mean gap (46 vs 54 s) but the realistic shape (p50 0.5 s vs 49 s), and a steady state instead of a cohort ramp. The SSD share falls from about 20% to about 2.5% because only human-scale pauses outlast L2's retention.
Models used. tiersim.py is the queue-aware model. On x70 it matched the tiered arm's wall time (86 vs 86-89 min) and mean TTFT (1.94 vs 1.48-1.94 s), counted a third fewer SSD returns than measured (13% vs 19.6%), and overstated collapsed arms by 1.35-2x. I drove it with /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/mine/evald.py (runs in cands_f.py, cands_h.py, gapclass.py, series2.py) and cross-checked with the unqueued stack-distance model wl_minreach/msim.py, which gives L1/L2/L3 = 0.89-0.90/0.08/0.024-0.025.
risks: The SSD signal is small: about 2.5% of returns, about 200-300 restores per arm, all after pauses of 5-10 min or more. Whole-window means will differ little between hbm_host and the three-tier arms (mean TTFT about 0.43 vs 0.19 s). Report by gap class (under 1, 1-5, 5-10, 10+ min, from gap_slept) and pair turns by (conv, turn); otherwise the result will read as 'the SSD does not matter'.

timeout and wait_complete should come out the same: the SSD is about 5% busy and a restore takes about 1.5 s, far below the timeout budget. That is the expected result for this regime, not a failed run. x70 remains the evidence for the contended case.

The gap law is grafted. TraceLab's think time comes from interactive developers using Claude Code and Codex, and here it is injected into autonomous SWE-bench conversations; TraceLab's tool latency also replaces the trace's own pre_gap. All L2 and L3 traffic follows from this assumption, so label the run 'interactive coding-agent cadence (TraceLab)'. Sensitivity check: keeping the trace's own gaps (x1) as the tool part raises the load by about 10% (1.64-1.66 turns/s) and puts hbm_host at its knee at C=80 (queue 0.2-1.3). Use C=72 for that variant.

The heavy-tailed think mixture makes the load depend on the seed: the mean gap ranges 43-50 s, so the load ranges 1.33-1.55 turns/s. Bake one seed into the trace for all four arms, and if time allows repeat hbm_host and one three-tier arm with a second seed.

hbm_lru collapses by construction, because L1 holds only about 40% of the working set: about 0.3 turns/s, about 2-min TTFT, and queue-time invalidation. It is capped at 7,200 s like the others; compare on the common window and do not read its TTFT as a cache effect. If a latency comparison against lru is needed, run C=64-72, where lru stays within capacity and the SSD share is 1.7-2.3%.

hbm_host runs at a moderate load (crude utilisation 0.8-0.9). If each hit turn costs more than the modelled 0.45 GPU-s, or decode is slower, it could approach its knee; at C=96 the model already shows a queue of 2-5. Run hbm_host first and watch the waiting queue from minute 30. If it stays above about 5 for more than 5 min, stop and rerun all arms at C=72.

Model error. Both models approximate LRU per session: they leave out page-level leaf-first eviction, protect_host, the L3 cleaner and write-through timing. On x70 the queue-aware model got the tiered arm right but counted a third fewer SSD returns than measured, so the real SSD share may be about 3-3.5%.

Four plumbing traps: (a) --gap-sample would give each arm different gaps, so bake the gaps into the trace. (b) run_compare.sh defaults of OFFSET=29, NCONV=48 and GAP_CAP=600 must be overridden; GAP_CAP must be 0, or the 30-min pauses are clipped to 10 min, exactly the L2/L3 boundary. (c) ARRIVAL passes through the environment but is not written to config.txt. (d) The server closes idle keep-alive connections after SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=5 s, so every request after a gap over 5 s (about 30% of turns) meets a stale pooled connection. The client retries once, but set SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE to 3600 or more, or use a force_close connector, to avoid aborted conversations like the two in campaign 7.

Warm-up. The first 30 min are the ramp and the first cohort aging, while W rises from 0.3M to about 1.6M; exclude them. The SSD share per 10-min window still varies from 1.5% to 3% depending on when pauses happen to fall, so report window totals with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Selection bias. The 283 conversations with at least 45 turns are all SWE-bench and longer than the corpus average. Contexts of 9.9K-57K tokens are mid-range compared with TraceLab's 119K median step, so the cost of one restore here (about 2.9 GB) understates Claude Code-scale contexts.
Disk. Each three-tier arm writes about 0.9 TB of KV to L3 (about 250 sessions x about 37K private tokens). That fits on the 2.27 TiB SSD below the 70% cleaner mark; keep the per-arm wipe.

alternatives.name: IDLE-80: idle-dominated upper bound (x60 cohort, i.e. LIT-80 as written)
alternatives.setting: 80 live sessions x 50 turns, taking the first 80 of the 228 conversations with exactly 50 turns in trace order, with no replacement (NCONV=C=80). Recorded gaps x60, capped at 600 s (GAP=60 GAP_CAP=600): mean about 46 s, p50 about 42 s. Poisson ramp at ARRIVAL=1.0; CLIENT_TIMEOUT 9000. No code change beyond the derived 50-turn trace. Queue-aware model: three-tier arms about 0.4 s mean TTFT; the SSD serves 6-10% of returns (15-20% of late turns); the working set peaks at about 2.1M for about 22 min. hbm_host collapses late (TTFT about 1 min) and hbm_lru collapses throughout.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use this when you need a strong SSD signal at 50 turns: to separate timeout from wait_complete, to load the SSD read path before building gap-time prefetch, or to add a lower-concurrency point to the x70/x10/x1 gap-scale series (it joins directly). Present it as the idle-dominated upper bound, not as realistic cadence.

alternatives.name: RT-96: realistic cadence at the hbm_host knee
alternatives.setting: The recommended recipe (283 conversations x up to 50 turns, TraceLab tool and think gaps baked in, ARRIVAL=0.1, 7,200 s) with C=96, near the AgentX narrative's 100 and HyperPod's 100 users. Model: 1.6-1.8 turns/s; working set about 2.0M (1.25x L2); SSD on 2.5-3.3% of returns (about 280-320 restores); hbm_host queue 2-5 with TTFT p90 6-10 s; hbm_lru collapsed.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use this if the C=80 run leaves too few SSD restores for tail percentiles, or if you want to watch hbm_host approach the queue-time invalidation regime under realistic cadence. It is the natural setting to test admission-time re-prefetch.

alternatives.name: LIT-DEFAULT: corpus-default replay (C=20-32, recorded gaps x1)
alternatives.setting: The 283-conversation pool, closed loop with replacement, TURNS=50, GAP=1 GAP_CAP=0 (recorded pre_gap, p50 0.71 s, no think pauses). C=20 (agentic-dataset) or C=32 (AgentX quick start), ARRIVAL=0.1, 5,400 s. Model: C=20 gives 1.8 turns/s, a 0.5M working set, 99.4% of tokens from L1 and no SSD use. C=32 gives 2.1-2.3 turns/s at capacity (queue about 3) with a 0.77M working set. All four arms come out identical.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use this when you need the standard benchmark point, to compare with published numbers, or as a sanity and regression run of the replay stack. It shows that at literature-default pacing this box is compute-bound and the host and SSD tiers sit idle. Do not use it to evaluate tiering.

judge.literature_summary:
Concurrency. Benchmarks keep a fixed number of live sessions in a closed loop and start a new conversation when one finishes. Verified settings:
- sammshen/agentic-dataset, the converter and run guide for this trace: 20.
- AIPerf InferenceX AgentX MVP: 32 in the quick start, 100 in the worked narrative; 15-30 min runs.
- MORI (UC Berkeley, arXiv 2606.00866): 20, 50 and 80 concurrent programs per replica, including one H200 running Qwen3-30B-A3B (this box's GPU and model). It replays Claude Code SWE-bench Pro traces with recorded tool durations for 1 h.
- SGLang HiCache blog, multi-turn example: 80 clients x 10 rounds.
- LMCache SageMaker HyperPod blog: 100 users at 8 QPS.
- AIPerf user-centric tutorial: 15 users at 1 req/s.
- LMCache MI300X blog (kv-cache-tester): 8 max users, plus a TTFT-gated ramp from 4 to 32 that peaked at 2-8 users.
- trace-collection-proxy: 10 sessions, and 500 on 4 GPUs.
- AA-AgentPerf: binary-searches the number of agents that meets per-agent speed SLOs.
Papers with open-loop arrivals use Poisson program arrivals instead: CachedAttention 1 session/s (ShareGPT, 5.75 turns), Continuum about 0.02-0.13 SWE-bench programs/s on one GPU, TokenCake 0.05-1 app/s. The typical range is 15-100 live sessions per node with 5-30 requests in flight. C=80 sits inside it: MORI's top level and the HiCache blog's client count.

Gaps. Measured gaps from the agent harness (tool time) have sub-second medians:
- This trace's pre_gap: p50 0.71 s, mean 2.0 s, p99 11.8 s, max 1,511 s. The HF datasets-server statistics agree (median 0.706 s, mean 2.02 s).
- trace-collection-proxy: p50 0.86 s, mean 1.49 s.
- TraceLab (UW, arXiv 2606.30560; 4,265 Claude Code and Codex sessions): tool latency p50 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s, p99 3.6 min, mean 18.4 s. Calls over 1 min are 4% of calls but 85% of tool time.
- AA-AgentPerf: tool delays from under 0.1 s to 5 s, median about 1 s.
- Continuum: SWE-bench tool time 0.93 ± 3.55 s.
- MORI: busy phases of short calls, separated by idle phases of tens of seconds to minutes (tests, human approval, subagents).
The only long gaps come from humans. TraceLab's think time is p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min, mean 46.7 min, it takes 92.3% of session wall-clock time, and a new user request comes every 8.8 LLM calls. Approval-gated suspensions last minutes to hours (JHU, arXiv 2608.30830).

Replay practice is real time. AgentX forbids per-trace or per-turn caps and compression (only a global 10 s idle guard). kv-cache-tester defaults to time-scale 1.0 with a 600 s max delay. MORI sleeps the recorded durations. No verified source stretches recorded gaps uniformly (x10, x60, x70). Where fixed synthetic periods are used, they are 2 s (agentic-dataset user-centric mode), 12.5 s (HyperPod) and 15 s (AIPerf).

TraceLab's tool latency plus one think pause per 8.8 calls (30-min cap) gives a mean idle time of about 46 s per call. That is the same mean as our x60-x70 runs, but the median is 0.5 s: the literature matches x70 in mean, not in shape. TraceLab's retention curve: prefix hit rate 85.4% at a 1-min TTL, about 94% at 5 min and 98.6% at 1 h; misses start at gaps over 5 min.

Turns and context.
- This trace: p50 34 turns, max 50; 228 conversations have exactly 50 and 283 have at least 45. Contexts grow from 9.9K to 43.6K tokens (p50) over 50 turns.
- TraceLab: 8.8 LLM calls per request and 73.6 tool-initiated steps per session on average. The median step is a 119K cached prefix + 875 new + 214 output tokens.
- Continuum SWE-bench: 10.9 turns and 70K tokens per program.
- AA-AgentPerf: input 5K-131K tokens, mean about 27K.
- LMCache MI300X Claude Code traces: 20K tokens at the start, 115K at the end.
- AIPerf tutorial: 20 turns. HyperPod: about 10-14 rounds.
Our 45-50-turn sessions of 9-57K tokens sit in the middle of this range.

What this means for this box. At literature-default pacing (C=20-32, recorded gaps) the live working set is 0.5-0.8M tokens, inside L1 or just above it, so L2 barely matters and the SSD never does (queue-aware model). The LMCache MI300X blog reports the same effect on its hardware: the CPU tier pays off only above a sustained working set of 250-300K tokens. The SSD becomes reachable only when sessions pause for human-scale times at about 80 sessions, where the working set passes L2's 1.63M tokens.
judge.related_work_for_prefetch_idea:
All items below were checked against the primary text; local copies are in the scratchpad.

A. Queue-lookahead prefetch, which acts only after the request has arrived.
- SGLang HiCache and Strata (arXiv 2508.18572; LMSYS HiCache blog): once a queued request's storage hit is detected, the storage-to-host prefetch runs during its queueing delay. Best-effort mode cancels it at dispatch, wait_complete stages the whole read, and timeout bounds it. These are the three-tier arms of our evaluation.
- CachedAttention / AttentionStore (USENIX ATC'24): 'scheduler-aware fetching' uses a look-ahead window over the job queue to move waiting jobs' KV from disk to host memory (window = free host capacity / mean session KV). 'Scheduler-aware eviction' exempts the KV of jobs inside a look-ahead eviction window and evicts from its tail. It works per session and pre-loads host-to-HBM layer by layer. Workload: ShareGPT, Poisson arrivals at 1 session/s, 128 GB DRAM and 10 TB SSD.
- PCR (arXiv 2603.23049, RAG): a look-ahead LRU that protects chunks needed by requests in the waiting queue, plus queue-based SSD-to-DRAM prefetching.
What this means for the idea: re-prefetching at admission and protecting a queued request's L2 chain for a bounded time (the fix for the x10/x1 queue-time invalidation) is the CachedAttention/PCR idea. The new part would be making it work on HiCache's page-level radix tree, with its write-through L2, shared prefixes, and prefetch_threshold/protect_host rules.

B. Prefetch before the request arrives, timed to the gap (the main idea).
- TokenCake (arXiv 2510.18586): when a function call starts, it offloads the stalled agent's KV from GPU to CPU (only if the freed memory is useful) and 'predictively uploads' it back ahead of the predicted call completion, reserving GPU blocks gradually. It needs an application graph API with call start and finish events. Its Table 2 labels CachedAttention's prefetch as reactive (on session resumption) and InferCept's as reactive (when the interception ends).
- KVFlow (arXiv 2507.07400): eviction ordered by steps-to-execution in the workflow, plus fully overlapped CPU-to-GPU prefetch for agents scheduled in the next step. Up to 1.83x and 2.19x faster than SGLang's hierarchical radix cache.
- SAGA (arXiv 2605.00528): a TTL that knows about tool calls, and speculative prefetch of the likely next step's prefix during tool execution, inspired by informed prefetching.
- PBKV (arXiv 2605.06472): lookahead eviction driven by workflow prediction, and conservative prefetch into otherwise idle GPU space.
- Symphony (arXiv 2412.16434): 'advisory requests' from the client (for example, a user starts typing) drive KV prefetch off the critical path and load balancing across machines. They arrive 11.3 s before the real request on ShareGPT and 5.8 s before it in MetaGPT.
- Signals: 'Ask the Tool, Don't Guess' (arXiv 2609.18849) shows that tool calls announce their last phase seconds before returning, 'enough to prefetch a context back into GPU memory'. TraceLab §7.4 proposes predicting gap durations and prefetching KV, and refreshing the cache during long human gaps.
- Industry roadmaps: NVIDIA Dynamo's agentic blog (Apr 2026) says 'the missing piece for agentic systems is prefetch' and that it is building harness hooks to bring blocks from storage to GPU ahead of the next request, alongside TTL pinning via cache_control and priority eviction. vLLM's AgentX blog (Sep 2026) lists prefetching retained KV toward the next turn's worker during the inter-turn gap as future work. SGLang RFC #27574 (Jun 2026) defines Share, Prefetch, Demote, Pin and Retain hints and has 'measure request-time L3 restoration before adding proactive Prefetch or Demote execution APIs' as an open TODO. RFC #36224 (Aug 2026) ships kv.prefetch only as restoration at request time, and makes pre-arrival transfer a non-goal until its scheduling, admission and telemetry requirements are specified.

C. Keeping KV resident instead of prefetching it.
- Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230, VLDB): pins KV in GPU memory through tool calls with a TTL computed from reload and queueing costs, and uses program-level FCFS to remove the per-turn queueing delay (the same delay behind our queue-time finding).
- InferCept (ICML'24): for each interception it chooses to preserve, discard or swap, with pipelined swapping; swap-in happens when the call returns.
- MORI (arXiv 2606.00866): places programs across GPU and DRAM by relative idleness, and promotes the least-idle CPU-resident program when GPU space frees.
- Pensieve (EuroSys'25): swaps out ahead of time and swaps in with pipelining.
- JHU cpu_ttl (arXiv 2608.30830): load-aware retention for suspensions that last as long as a human approval.
- Counterpoint: 'Where Should the KV Cache Live?' (arXiv 2609.16215, a simulator study) finds that lookahead prefetch never paid for its bandwidth in its grid.
- Foundations: informed prefetching and caching (Patterson et al., SOSP'95), and integrated prefetching and caching (Cao, Felten, Karlin and Li, SIGMETRICS'95; Kimbrel et al., OSDI'96): prefetching too early evicts blocks that were still useful.

How the idea differs.
1. Tier and cost. It moves KV from SSD to host (L3 to L2) at 1.88 GiB/s. One context of about 30K tokens is about 2.9 GB: about 1.5 s at the ceiling, or 2.6-3.3 s p50 under contention. TokenCake, KVFlow, SAGA, PBKV and Symphony move CPU to GPU. Here lead time and the SSD bandwidth budget become first-class concerns.
2. Trigger. The prefetch starts before the request arrives, from tool-call or think events or a gap predictor. HiCache, Strata, CachedAttention and PCR start only after the request is queued.
3. Budget. With the working set about equal to L2, every prefetched context evicts another session's KV, so the idea needs a rule that decides prefetch and eviction together. In RT-80, L2 effectively retains a session for about 6-10 min, so prefetching during the gap pays only for returns predicted after a longer gap.
4. It combines with re-checking queued requests at admission, which is a HiCache version of CachedAttention's scheduler-aware eviction.
5. None of the verified work evaluates gap-time SSD-to-host prefetch on a replayed agentic trace with a measured three-tier write-through hierarchy. The SGLang RFC asks for exactly that measurement before building proactive prefetch.

Upside bound. In RT-80, about 2-3% of returns (the turns right after a pause, where a human is waiting) pay about 1.5 s for an SSD restore instead of about 0.2 s from L2. In the idle-dominated x70 regime about 20% of returns did.

That curve could directly validate the 'L1 about 1 min, L2 6-10 min' retention claim; tiersim was only calibrated on aggregates. The same files hold measured service times: x70 three_tier_to gave 44.7 ms/token and 10.2 s mean turn latency at 1.88 turns/s (about 19 in flight), and 28-33 ms/token at 2-4 in flight.

There is no statistical design: no replication and no power estimate for about 190-300 SSD restores per arm. The two three-tier arms are expected to be identical, so they should be pre-registered as a replicate that gives the run-to-run noise floor. Per-class bootstrap intervals should also be planned before launch.

Session heterogeneity is not modelled. In TraceLab Table 7 the per-session human-think p50 is 0.0 s and the median session lasts 5.1 min: most real sessions are single-request. The recipe gives every 50-call session about 5.7 i.i.d. pauses. It has no busy/idle phase clustering (which MORI describes) and no sensitivity run for per-session pause clustering.
doubtful_claims: The TraceLab tool-latency parameters do not match the current arXiv HTML (2606.30560). Its Table 7 per-step tool execution is avg 16.8 s, p50 0.1 s, p90 10.0 s, p99 3.2 min; the 0.3 s p50 appears only in the per-request row, where p90 is 2.3 min. The recommendation's 0.3 s / 13.6 s / 3.6 min / 18.4 s may come from another version or row. The median Claude step prefix is 126,180 tokens (Codex 115,584), not 119K. Human think (p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min, mean 46.7 min, 92.3% idle) and hit-vs-TTL (85.4% / about 94% / 98.6%; misses begin past 5 min) do match. The effect on tier results is small, because tool gaps are served from L1, but refit or relabel before calling this 'the best-anchored gap law'.

'The mean matches TraceLab's idle time per LLM call (about 46 s)' holds only after the caps. The capped tool lognormal has a mean of 8.5 s against TraceLab's 16.8-18.4 s, and the capped think has a mean of 5.5 min against 46.7 min. Even uncapped, the p50/p90 lognormal gives a think mean of 12.6 min, so it misfits the tail. TraceLab's 92.3% idle figure includes multi-day breaks (per-session p99 190 h). Under the recipe humans are idle about 69% of wall-clock (0.114 x 328 / 54.5). The 30-min cap is a defensible choice, since anything over 10 min goes to L3 anyway, but the 'same mean as x70' equivalence comes from the cap, not from the data.

The restore size is overstated: 'each restore ~30K tokens (~2.9 GB), ~1.5 s; ~0.5 TB read per arm'. The system prompt stays in L1, and leaf-first eviction leaves part of the prefix in L2. An independent session-LRU check (scratchpad/critic/lrucheck.py) gives 19.2-19.8K L3 tokens per restore, i.e. about 1.9 GB and about 1.0 s at the ceiling, or about 0.35-0.55 TB read per arm. That is roughly 1.5x lower than stated. The same check does confirm about 1.47-1.56 turns/s, 2.4-2.8% L3 share (seeds 1-3), 2.2% at C=72, 3.2% at C=96, and L2 eviction age p10-p90 of 5.5-10.4 min.

'5-10 min gaps: about a quarter go to the SSD' is fragile across seeds: the L3 fraction of that class is 0.24, 0.54 and 0.48 for seeds 1-3 in the independent check. Only the 10-min-and-over class (about 100% L3) is robust, so conclusions per class should rest on it.

The keep-alive risk is overstated: 'every request after a gap over 5 s (about 30% of turns) meets a stale pooled connection'. Own data contradicts it. Across the 12 NAT160 arms of campaigns 7-9 there were 3 connection errors in total: 2 aborts in c7 three_tier_wc and 1 retry in c8 three_tier_wc. aiohttp drops idle connections the server has closed, so this is a rare close/reuse race. Raising SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE (a real variable, default 5, python/sglang/srt/environ.py:325) is harmless but does not fix a 30% problem.

The subset description is wrong: 'all SWE-bench, originally minimax-m2.5; every conversation shares a 7,808-token system prompt'. The 283 conversations with at least 45 turns are 235 minimax-m2.5, 34 deepseek-v3.1 and 14 claude-sonnet-4-6. Message 0 has 2 distinct system prompts (269 share one). One pair shares an identical first user message, a duplicated task.

The service-time assumption is optimistic: 31-35 ms ITL with about 12 in flight, so S is 7-9 s. x70 measured 44.7 ms/token and a 10.2 s mean turn latency at 1.88 turns/s. Expect S of about 9-10 s and N of about 13-15. X falls only about 3% (to about 1.43), but hbm_host's margin to its knee and the in-flight KV are a little worse than stated.

The realism argument is inconsistent. x60 is rejected because AgentX forbids re-timing and 'no source stretches recorded gaps', yet RT-80 replaces every recorded gap with synthetic draws, which is not replay under the same rule. Present RT-80 as a synthetic cadence calibrated to TraceLab, not as literature replay practice.

'C=80 equals MORI's top concurrency on an H200 with Qwen3-30B-A3B' matches only the concurrency number. MORI sleeps recorded Claude Code tool durations (no injected human think) at longer contexts, so its offered load and working set are not comparable.

proposals.name: C80 x 50 turns, TraceLab tool+think gaps (smallest load that reaches the SSD)
proposals.gap_model: Each (conv, turn>0) gets a deterministic, seeded gap. It is written into a derived trace with pre_gap overwritten and replayed with GAP=1 and GAP_CAP=0, so all 4 arms sleep the same gap on the same turn. Do not use --gap-sample: it draws from one shared RNG in completion order, so the sequence differs between arms. The gap is still measured from the end of the reply. It has two parts. (1) Tool time, drawn every turn: min(216 s, LogNormal(median 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s)), sigma 2.98. That is TraceLab Table 7 tool latency, capped at its p99 of 3.6 min; capped mean 8.5 s. (2) Think time, added with probability p = 1/8.8 = 0.114 (TraceLab: 8.8 LLM calls per user request): min(1,800 s, LogNormal(median 84 s, p90 1,236 s)), sigma 2.10. That is TraceLab human think time. The 30-min cap keeps about 93% of these gaps unchanged; the capped mean is 328 s. Resulting per-turn gap: p10 0.01 s, p50 0.49 s, p75 5.6 s, p90 61 s, p95 216 s, p99 1,456 s, mean 45.9 s. 10% of gaps exceed 1 min, 3.2% exceed 5 min, 2.0% exceed 10 min and 1.2% exceed 20 min. The trace's own pre_gap at x1 (p50 0.71 s, mean 2.08 s) has almost the same median as the tool part. It does not work alone because it has no think tail: at any load this box can sustain, the SSD is never reached (see the arithmetic).
proposals.arrival_model: Session arrivals start as a Poisson ramp at 0.1 conversations/s (ARRIVAL=0.1), capped at 80 live (--concurrency 80). The 80 slots fill in about 13 min. After that it is a closed loop: a session holds its slot across its gaps, and a finished session is replaced at once by the next unused conversation. The pool is the 228 trace conversations with exactly 50 turns (TURNS=50), each used at most once per arm, since the client cannot bust the cache. Per-arm wall cap is MAX_SECONDS=7200; the pool runs dry at about 2 h anyway. Analysis window: 15 to 120 min. Pair turns across arms by (conv, turn), and read the tier effect by deterministic gap class (for example gap >= 10 min), not by the tier each arm happened to observe.
proposals.conversation_selection: Use the 228 conversations with exactly 50 turns (of 768), in trace order, OFFSET=0. Put them in the same derived trace file that carries the deterministic gaps, because replay_agentic.py has no min-turns filter. Every session builds up its full history. Context p50 at turns 1 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 50: 9.9K / 18.8K / 25.3K / 37.3K / 43.7K tokens. Final context mean 45.6K (p10 35K, p90 57.6K). The 7,808-token system prompt is shared by all sessions. Private KV per session: 21.3K tokens averaged over its lifetime, about 37.8K at turn 50. Caveat: these are the long SWE-bench tasks that used up the 50-step budget, so the pool is biased toward long tasks.
proposals.expected_utilization: These are predictions. Three-tier arms: about 0.6 of GPU capacity (1.35 turns/s x 0.45 GPU-s per hit turn). At x70 the three-tier arm stayed stable at 1.8 turns/s in its steady window, so there is margin. hbm_host: about 0.8, because 2.5% of returns recompute about 29K tokens at about 6.3 s each; across seeds the range is 0.77 to 0.87. hbm_lru: about 1.4, because 10% of returns recompute. The closed loop then throttles it to about 1.0 turns/s, which adds about 20 s of queueing per turn (80/0.97 - 60 s cycle). That is mild overload, not the 100-150 s queues of x10/x1. SSD: about 5% read-busy (0.03 restores/s x ~2.9 GB) and about 8% write-busy (write-through of ~1.1K new tokens per turn, about 0.15 GB/s). Running requests take about 12 x 30K = 0.37M of the 668K-token L1.
proposals.expected_L3_reach: About 2.5% of returning turns (range 2.2-2.7% across seeds) have their prefix only on the SSD. That is about 190 SSD restores per arm in the 15-120 min window, out of about 8,400 steady turns. About 8% come from L2 (about 650) and about 90% from L1. The split follows the gap classes. L1 returns come after tool gaps (gap p50 0.3 s, p90 12 s). L2 returns come after think gaps with p50 of about 2-3 min (p10 1 min, p90 6 min). SSD returns come after think gaps with p50 of about 15-22 min (p10 about 10 min). A long gap reaches the SSD because the LRU distance during it covers the whole live set (80 x 21.3K = 1.70M, which is at least L2 = 1.63M) plus the KV of sessions that finished during the gap. This matches TraceLab's measured pattern: misses begin at gaps over 5 min, and nearly everything misses past 1 h. The model is calibrated on the x70 campaign. There it predicted L1/L2/L3 of .28/.49/.22 and 1.93 turns/s, against measured .25/.49/.24 and 1.8 turns/s in the steady window. Sensitivity: L2 10% smaller gives L3 3.1%; C=64 gives 1.7%; C=96 gives 2.7-3.0%.

proposals.arithmetic:
1) Capacity to beat. L2 is write-through, so it is a superset of L1: unique two-tier capacity = L2 = 1,627,648 tokens. The shared 7,808-token prefix counts once. A 50-turn session's private KV averages 21.3K over its lifetime (37.8K at turn 50). When session ages are mixed, live WS ~ C x 21.3K. The live set alone exceeds L2 when C >= 1.63M / 21.3K = 76.
2) Literature-typical load does not reach the SSD. At C=20-32 with the trace gaps at x1 (mean 2.1 s), live WS is 0.50-0.77M, below or at L1. Modelled L1/L2/L3 = .99/.01/.00, and C=32 already needs rho of about 1.0. At real tool gaps this box can only serve about 20-30 sessions, and they all fit in HBM. The x10/x1 runs at C=128 were oversubscribed for this reason.
3) To have 80 sessions and stay under capacity, each session must be slow. Take the target rate lambda of about 1.3-1.4 turns/s. That is about 75% of the 1.8 turns/s the three-tier arm sustained at x70, where hbm_host was already queueing. Cycle = 80 / 1.35 = 59 s. With loaded service of about 9 s (TTFT 0.3-2 s plus 211 output tokens at about 25 tok/s under chunked-prefill interference), the mean gap needs to be about 50 s. The measured tool+think mixture gives 45.9 s: 8.5 s of tool time plus 0.114 x 328 s of think time. That lands near the target without a free scale factor.
4) Offered rate: lambda = 80 / (9.2 + 46) = 1.35 turns/s. The simulator gives 1.27-1.44 across 5 seeds. In flight = 1.35 x 9.2 = 12.4 requests.
5) Working set: 80 x 21.3K + 7.8K = 1.71M. The simulated time average is 1.61-1.66M, with peaks of 1.8-2.0M. That is 1.0x L2 and 2.5x L1. Dead-session KV adds LRU pressure during long gaps.
6) Tier reach, from an LRU stack-distance model calibrated on x70: 90% of returns from L1, 8% from L2, 2.5% from SSD. SSD returns are about 0.03/s, about 190 in the 105-min steady window.
7) GPU load, with c_hit = 0.45 GPU-s and c_recompute = 29K / 4903 + 0.3 = 6.3 s:
   - three-tier: 1.35 x 0.45 = 0.61
   - hbm_host: 1.35 x (0.975 x 0.45 + 0.025 x 6.3) = 0.80
   - hbm_lru: 1.35 x (0.90 x 0.45 + 0.10 x 6.3) = 1.40. Its closed loop throttles to X of about 0.97, and the response time grows by N/X - Z = 82 - 60 = about 22 s.
8) SSD:
   - restore of 30K tokens = 2.9 GB / 1.88 GiB/s = 1.5 s
   - reads: 0.03/s x 2.9 GB = about 5% busy
   - writes: 1.35 x 1.1K tokens x 98,304 B = 0.15 GB/s, about 8%
   - timeout-policy budget: 1.0 + 0.25 x 29.3 = 8.3 s, well above 1.5 s, so the timeout should rarely fire and TO vs WC should differ little.
9) Duration: ramp 80 / 0.1 = 13 min. The pool offers 228 x 50 = 11,400 turns, of which about 9,700 fall within the 7,200 s cap for a three-tier arm (8,400 in the steady window). 4 arms x 2 h + boots = about 8.5 h, versus about 23 h for campaigns 7-9.
10) Brackets. C=64: rho .48/.59/.99, SSD 1.7%, about 130 restores, too few for a p90. C=96: rho .72/.96/1.79, SSD 2.7%, but hbm_host is back at the edge of the queue-invalidation regime. C=80 is the smallest C with enough SSD events that keeps both host-pool arms below saturation.
risks: The think-time part comes from TraceLab's interactive developers and is injected into autonomous SWE-bench conversations. It is the only source of L2 and SSD traffic, so every tier result depends on that assumption. The recorded trace gaps alone (x1) never reach the SSD at a load this box can sustain. Report the result as 'interactive agent cadence', not 'faithful replay of this trace'.

The SSD is small in aggregate: only about 2.5% of returns, about 190 per arm. Mean TTFT across all turns will differ little between hbm_host and the three-tier arms. The per-tier answer has to come from paired, conditioned analysis: same (conv, turn) across arms, bucketed by the deterministic gap class (<1 min, 1-10 min, >=10 min). An aggregate mean alone could wrongly read as 'the SSD doesn't matter'.

The prefetch-policy arms are expected to be indistinguishable. The SSD is about 5% busy and a restore takes about 1.5 s, far below the 8.3 s timeout budget. If three_tier_to and three_tier_wc come out equal, that is the expected result, not a failed experiment. Separating them needs a targeted burst: synchronised long-gap returns or a smaller prefetch timeout.

hbm_lru at rho of about 1.4 will queue. Queue time lengthens the effective reuse distance, so more L1 misses, then more recompute, which could spiral past the predicted ~20 s. hbm_host at 0.77-0.87 could tip over if the real cost per hit turn exceeds 0.45 GPU-s. Watch the queue depth in the first 30 min. If hbm_host holds a queue above about 10, the queue-time invalidation regime of x10/x1 is back.

Model error. The session-granularity LRU model ignores page-level, leaf-first eviction, in-flight lock pinning, protect_host and the L3 cleaner. It matched x70 to within 3 points, but these realistic gaps put every miss in a thin tail, so relative error on the 2.5% SSD share is larger (2.2-3.1% across seeds and an L2 10% smaller).

Conversation pool and warm-up. Only 228 fifty-turn conversations exist, and each can be used at most once per arm (no cache-bust), so the pool runs dry at about 2 h. The first cohort of 80 starts within 13 min and ages together. Exclude the first 15 min, and treat the last 10-15 min as drain if the cap is not reached. Slower arms complete fewer turns before the cap, so compare only the common (conv, turn) set.

Implementation. The gaps must be precomputed per (conv, turn) into a derived trace file. The existing --gap-sample option would give each arm a different gap sequence, because its RNG is shared and drawn in completion order. The derived file also replaces the missing min-turns filter. Keep ignore_eos with the recorded output lengths and the same pools on all four arms, so this campaign can be joined with x70/x10/x1.

proposals.name: LIT-80: 80 live sessions x 50 turns, recorded gaps x60 capped at 600 s, cohort start ramped at 1 session/s
proposals.conversation_selection: Use only the 228 conversations that have exactly 50 turns (all swebench), kept in trace order. Write them to a derived data file (traces/lmcache_agentic_trace_262k_50t.json) and take the first 80: NCONV=80, OFFSET=0, TURNS=50. No code change is needed. That window's mean final context is 46.6K tokens, against 45.6K for all 228 (p10 35.3K, p90 57.3K, max 109K, all below CTX=131072). Because every chosen conversation has 50 turns, all 80 sessions stay live until they finish, and the live count only falls in the tail. Reuse the same file and window for all 4 arms.
proposals.gap_model: gap = recorded pre_gap x 60, with each gap capped at 600 s (GAP=60, GAP_CAP=600). Each gap is fixed per (conversation, turn), so all four arms see identical gaps. Over the 50-turn set this gives mean 47.9 s, p10 3.6 s, p50 42.5 s, p90 74.6 s and p99 408 s. 0.78% of gaps hit the cap. Total idle time per session is p50 2,244 s, p90 3,196 s and max 5,880 s. Why x60: TraceLab gives a mean idle time per LLM call of about 39-64 s. That figure is (7.8 tool gaps at a mean of 18.4 s + 1 human pause per request) / 8.8 calls, where the human pause has a median of 84 s and a p90 of 20.6 min and is capped at 10-60 min. x60 puts the mean near the middle of that range. A uniform time scale plus a per-gap cap is the knob kv-cache-tester offers (--time-scale, and --max-delay with a default of 600 s). The main difference from literature practice: AgentX and agentic-dataset replay the recorded gaps at x1 with no caps.
proposals.arrival_model: Closed loop with 80 live sessions. NCONV = C = 80, so there are no replacements; each session holds its slot through its gaps. Session starts follow a seeded Poisson process at 1.0 conversation/s (ARRIVAL=1.0, SEED=0; C=80 is only a cap and never binds), so all 80 are live within about 80 s. This avoids the synchronized turn-0 burst and stands in for AgentX's staggered start and kv-cache-tester's ramp. The result is a cohort ramp, not a steady state: the working set grows with turn index. The per-arm wall cap is CLIENT_TIMEOUT = MAX_SECONDS = 5,400 s. Compare arms over the common window, as in RUNBOOK 7.3. run_compare.sh does not export ARRIVAL, so pass it in the environment (ARRIVAL=1.0 bash run_compare.sh) and add it to config.txt by hand.
proposals.expected_L3_reach: About 9% of returning turns overall should need the SSD, rising to about 15-20% in the last 40% of turns. Each such return restores about 25K tokens (2.5 GB). These numbers come from a session-level LRU stack-distance model of an inclusive L1/L2: a return goes to L3 when the context touched more recently than its own last use is larger than L2. On the campaign-7 x70 setup (C=128, 40 turns) the same model predicted 15-19% SSD returns, and 19.6% was measured, so it is calibrated. The reason reach stays modest: the working set is below L2 until about turn 24 and reaches only 1.9x L2 at turn 50, and LRU keeps every session whose gap is shorter than L2's residence time. The result also depends on the window and on decode speed: across different windows and decode speeds the model gives 7.5-10.7%, and 3% for one bad window. In hbm_host the same returns become recomputes. In the late phase that is about 1.3 x 0.17 x 25.7K ≈ 5.7K tok/s, more than the 4,903 tok/s prefill rate, so hbm_host should saturate in the second half. hbm_lru recomputes most of each of about 69% of returns and saturates early, at about 0.5-0.6 turns/s as in campaigns 8 and 9.
proposals.expected_utilization: Tiered arms: about 1.3 turns/s offered. That is about 72% of the 1.77 turns/s the SSD arms sustained with queue 0-7 in the campaign-7 x70 main window, and about 45-65% of the estimated 2-3 turns/s hit-dominated capacity. The binding limit is device memory, not compute. About 14 requests are in flight; late in the run each holds about 46K of context, and the model puts running KV at p95 670-790K against the 668K L1 pool. So late in the run admission reaches the memory limit, much as in campaign 7, which the model placed at p95 745K. SSD read in the late phase is about 0.56 GB/s (28% of the 2.02 GB/s ceiling), and L3 write-through is about 0.1 GB/s. hbm_host goes above 1 in the late phase (recompute alone exceeds prefill capacity). hbm_lru is above 1 for most of the run.
literature_anchors: sammshen/agentic-dataset README (the converter and run guide for this same trace): --concurrency 20 live sessions, the recorded delay = pre_gap replayed, ignore_eos. This is the de-facto default for this corpus.

proposals.arithmetic:
0) Box check of the literature settings, using the calibrated simulator (scratchpad sim.py over the real turn sizes and gaps). C=32 at x1 over 50 turns: demand about 2.0 turns/s (at or above the 1.77 demonstrated), about 18 requests in flight, working set W at most 1.32M < L2, 83% of returns fully served from L1, 0% SSD. That is a compute-saturation test like campaign 9. C=20 at x1: W at most 0.83M, 99% L1 hits. C=15 with a 15 s gap: W about 0.7M, about the size of L1. TraceLab-shaped gaps (x1 tool gaps plus a human pause with probability 1/8.8, median 84 s, capped at 30 min) at C=80-96: 1.15-1.33 turns/s, about 90% L1 hits, SSD reach only 1.4-1.9%. The bare threshold C=64 at x70: W max 2.53M but SSD reach 1%. Conclusion: W > L2 is necessary but not sufficient. W has to stay above L2 for a large part of the run.
1) Time per turn on a loaded box: TTFT about 0.3 s plus 213 mean output tokens at 20-25 tok/s per sequence. Campaign 7 x70 measured 12.4 s mean latency per turn, so S ≈ 9-12 s.
2) Mean gap G at x60 with a 600 s cap, over the 50-turn set: 47.9 s.
3) Throughput X = C/(G+S) = 80/(47.9+11) ≈ 1.36 turns/s. The simulator gives 1.28-1.33 over the t10-t90 window.
4) In flight N = X·S ≈ 1.3 x 11 ≈ 14, or 12-16 in simulation.
5) Running KV late in the run ≈ 14 x 46.6K ≈ 650K against 668K of L1. This is at the device-memory admission limit; campaign 7 ran at a similar margin and stayed stable.
6) Unique working set W(t) = 7,808 + 80 x (context - 7,808): turn 1 ≈ 0.16M; turn 20 ≈ 80 x 17.9K = 1.44M. W crosses L2 when context > 7,808 + (1,627,648 - 7,808)/80 = 28.1K, around turn 24. Turn 30 ≈ 1.99M (1.2x L2), turn 40 ≈ 2.5M (1.5x), turn 50 = 3.11M (1.91x). Median over the run is about 1.64M, roughly the size of L2.
7) L3 reach from the LRU stack-distance model: about 9% of returns overall and 15-20% late, about 25K tokens per SSD-touching return. On campaign 7 the model predicted 15-19% against 19.6% measured.
8) SSD bandwidth late in the run: 1.3 x 0.17 x 25.7K x 98,304 B ≈ 0.56 GB/s, 28% of 2.02 GB/s. Write-through: 1.3 x (515 new + 213 output) tokens x 98 KB ≈ 0.09 GB/s.
9) Baselines: hbm_host recompute late ≈ 1.3 x 0.17 x 25.7K ≈ 5.7K tok/s, above the 4,903 tok/s prefill rate, so it saturates. In hbm_lru only 31% of returns are fully served from L1, so it saturates early.
10) Duration: per session ≈ 2,244 s of gap (p50) + 50 x 11 s ≈ 2,800 s. t90 ≈ 2,550-2,700 s, and 99.8% of the tiered arms' turns are done by 5,400 s. With a 5,400 s cap per arm, 4 arms plus boots and L3 wipes take about 6.3 h. By comparison, campaign 7 x70 (C=128, 40 turns) ran at 1.8 turns/s with about 22 in flight; this design offers 28% less load with 37% fewer sessions and 25% more turns.
risks: The design sits near a knee. The median working set is about L2 (1.64M), so SSD reach depends on the window and on decode speed: the model gives 7.5-10.7%, and 3% for one bad window. Check W(t) for the chosen window before running. If you need a stronger SSD signal, the literature-consistent fallbacks are C=88 at x70 (reach 17-19%, 1.27-1.33 turns/s, mean gap 55 s) or C=96 at x80 (17-25%, 1.25 turns/s, mean gap 62 s).

Device memory binds before compute. Fifty turns means contexts of about 46K at the end (p90 57K), and about 14 in flight fill the 668K L1. Late in the run, admission waits could rebuild a queue and bring back the queue-time L2 invalidation seen in campaigns 8 and 9, even in the tiered arms. Watch queue depth: more than about 10 sustained means the run has left the stable regime.

The gap shape does not match the literature. A uniform x60 makes every gap long (p50 42 s), while real agent harnesses and TraceLab show mostly sub-second tool gaps with rare long pauses. With TraceLab-shaped gaps, L1 serves about 90% of returns and SSD reach drops to about 2%. Report this design as the idle-dominated regime (TraceLab: users are idle 92% of the time), which is an upper bound on the SSD tier's value.

Concurrency 80 is at the high end of the literature. Typical single-node settings are 15-32 live sessions at recorded, sub-second pacing, and on this box those give W ≤ 1.3M (below L2), making them a throughput test in which L3 cannot matter. Say this explicitly when presenting the result.

This is a cohort ramp, not a steady state. Sessions start within about 80 s and grow together, so the SSD effect falls in turns 24-50. Report results by turn-index bucket (or by W/L2), not only as whole-run means. A steady-state replay with replacement (AgentX style) would need about 150 live sessions to reach the same W, because the mean context over a session's life is only about 29K.
Selection bias: only the 228 conversations with exactly 50 turns are used, all swebench, so contexts and gap tails are longer than the corpus average.

hbm_host and hbm_lru are expected to saturate and hit the 5,400 s cap. Their means are then capped-window numbers, so compare over the common window. The cap also drops about 0.2% of tiered turns (the few sessions with about 5,900 s of total gap).

The model assumes 20-25 tok/s decode under load (calibrated on campaign 7) and no queueing. If decode is faster at this lower load, in-flight falls and throughput rises by a few percent. If queueing appears, the reach estimate no longer holds.
Transport resets end a conversation after one retry (campaign 7 lost 2 of them this way), which shrinks the live set a little. ARRIVAL is not recorded in config.txt by run_compare.sh.

proposals.name: c72-t50-ln40: 72 live sessions × 50 turns, lognormal gaps with a 40 s median, Poisson ramp at 0.5 sessions/s
proposals.gap_model: Each (conversation, turn) gets its own independent lognormal gap: median 40 s, sigma 0.8, capped at 600 s. Resulting spread: mean 55.1 s, p10 14.3 s, p90 111.5 s, p99 257 s, CV 0.95. The cap applies to only 0.04% of gaps. Turn 0 has no gap. As before, a gap runs from the end of the previous reply to the next send. The gaps are drawn once from a fixed seed and written into the pre_gap field of a derived trace, which is replayed with GAP=1 and GAP_CAP=600. That way every arm sees the same gap for each (conversation, turn). Do not use --gap-sample for this: it draws from one shared RNG in completion order, so each arm would get different gaps. Why not the recorded trace gaps scaled up: in the 50-turn conversations the per-conversation mean gap is 0.50 s at p10, 0.77 s at p50 and 6.8 s at p90. That spread desynchronizes the cohort, and scaled-trace variants reached the SSD on only 1-7% of returns (C=72-80 at x60-x80). The lognormal gives every session the same gap distribution.
proposals.arrival_model: Closed loop with 72 live sessions and no replacement (NCONV = C = 72, a cohort). Sessions open as a Poisson ramp at 0.5 per second (ARRIVAL=0.5, with C=72 as the cap), so all 72 are open after about 2.4 minutes. The arrival RNG is seeded, so every arm gets the same ramp. Each session then runs its 50 turns in order, separated by its baked gaps. The run has three phases: about 0-25 min in L1/L2 only, about 25-45 min where the SSD is used, and a drain after about 40 min. Expected wall time for each tiered arm is 63-77 min.
proposals.expected_L3_reach: About 8-11% of returning turns should need an SSD restore: 281-397 restores out of 3,528 returns per tiered arm, averaging about 27K tokens (2.6 GB) each, 0.7-1.1 TB read per arm. Before turn ~25 the share is 0. For turns 30 and later it is 16-23%. Why: the live unique working set crosses L2 (1.63M tokens) at about 25 min (turn ~30) and peaks at 2.06-2.19M tokens, 1.27-1.35x L2. It stays above L2 for about 20-23 min. In that window, a return misses L2 once the other sessions have touched more than L2's worth of KV since this session was last used. That happens when λ(g+R)w ≥ 1.63M; with λ≈1.1 turns/s and w≈30K tokens, the gap must exceed ~43 s, which is 46% of lognormal draws. LRU recency and the drain reduce the share actually realized. For comparison, x70 had ~19% of returns from the SSD. hbm_host has to recompute about 21-27% of returns, because queueing makes the evictions compound.
literature_anchors: sammshen/agentic-dataset (the converter for our exact trace): recommends --concurrency 20 live sessions, or user-centric mode with 20 users at 10 QPS (a 2 s turn gap). An earlier commit used concurrency 128, but that meant in-flight requests, not sessions.

AIPerf InferenceX AgentX MVP: --concurrency 32 live session trees in the quick start and 100 in the worked narrative. It replays recorded gaps with no per-trace or per-turn caps, and only a global 10 s idle guard.

proposals.arithmetic:
1. Why the literature settings cannot be used unchanged: the published setups run 15-32 live sessions with 2-15 s gaps, or real-time trace pacing (trace gap mean ~2 s). On this box, 32 sessions × 37.8K private tokens is only 1.21M tokens, which fits in L2 (1.63M), so the SSD would never be touched. At real-time pacing (G≈2 s, R≈7 s), the box sustains only 12-18 sessions (λ = C/(G+R) ≤ ~2 turns/s). That matches the 4-8-user plateau in the LMCache MI300X blog. Using the SSD with a fixed 160 GB L2 therefore requires an idle-heavy workload.
2. Working set: I used the 228 conversations that have exactly 50 turns. Their mean private context (prompt + reply − 7,808 shared tokens) is 24.8K at turn 30, 31.2K at turn 40 and 37.8K at turn 50. The shared prefix counts once. A synchronized cohort would give C × 37.8K, i.e. 2.72M for C=72. But session end times spread over about ±20% (mostly from differing output lengths and the sum of 49 gaps), so the live working set peaks at only ~0.76-0.8 of that. This corrects the '>47 sessions at 50 turns' rule of thumb. At C=64 the simulated peak is 1.6-1.8M, about equal to L2, and only 0.3-3% of returns reached the SSD. At C=72 the peak is 2.06-2.19M (1.27-1.35x L2), with 8-11% of returns reaching the SSD. C=72 is therefore the smallest cohort that clears L2 with some margin.
3. Service time: the effective ITL under HiCache fits ≈ 24 + 0.55·N ms, from campaign-7 three_tier_wc (37-42 ms at 14-22 in flight, 26 ms at 2). A turn decodes 218 tokens on average, at ~28 ms per token with N≈7, which is ~6 s. Prefill of the ~530-token new input takes ~0.1 s. So R ≈ 6.5-8 s when unqueued.
4. Capacity: in a saturation run (gap 0, 64 sessions, hit-dominated), the model gives 2.9-3.5 turns/s at turns 9-21 (10-19K contexts), 2.35 at turn ~31 and ~1.9 at turn ~35+. At late contexts, the L1 pool (668K) holds only ~16-20 running requests. Once a queue persists with the working set above L2, the model collapses to ~0.2 turns/s through queue-time invalidation. That is the x10/x1 failure. The same model reproduces the measured x70 result (tiered arm 1.9 s mean vs 1.5-1.9 s measured; 13-19% of returns from the SSD; 86 min) and the x10 collapse (tiered arm = host arm, ~53% recompute).
5. Gap from Little's law: λ = C/(G+R). Choosing λ ≈ 1.1-1.2 turns/s (about 50-60% of late capacity) and C=72 gives G+R ≈ 60-65 s, so the mean gap G is about 55 s. A lognormal with median 40 s and sigma 0.8 has mean 55 s. Its tail (p99 257 s) stays within TraceLab's 5-min 'still cached' horizon.
6. Offered load in the model (3 seeds): 1.21-1.23 turns/s peak over 5 min, 1.14 falling to 0.8 over the turn≥30 windows, and 0.78-0.95 averaged over the whole run. Mean in-flight is 5.7-6.9 (late phase ~5-6). Queue ≈ 0. The GPU spends ~10% of its time in prefill.
7. SSD load: restores of ~27K tokens at 20.5K tok/s (the 1.88 GiB/s read ceiling) take ~1.3 s each at full bandwidth. Predicted SSD read utilization is 8-14%, and predicted TTFT for returns restored from the SSD is 2.3-2.7 s mean. Predicted tiered-arm TTFT overall is 0.33-0.46 s mean and 0.1 s p50.
8. Arms without the SSD: hbm_host has to recompute the part beyond L2 (~27K tokens, ~5.5 s of prefill each). That adds ~1.1 × 0.2 × 5.5 ≈ 1.2 s of GPU work per second, which exceeds capacity, so it queues in the late phase. Predicted: TTFT mean 47-67 s, p50 0.2 s, 139-154 min. hbm_lru: TTFT ~115 s mean, 67% recompute, ~260 min.
9. How stable this point is: the model shows no collapse in 8 of 8 seeds at the base setting, and 1 collapse in 32 stressed seeds (ITL ×1.4, L1 ×0.8, or ITL ×1.2 with L1 ×0.9). Shorter gaps sit closer to the edge: median 30-35 s at C=72 collapsed in 1-3 of 8 stressed seeds, and C=80 at median 40 s collapsed in 1 of 3 unstressed seeds. So this is the least extreme setting that is still robust.
10. How it compares with x70 (128 sessions × 40 turns, gap p50 49 s, mean 54 s, cap 1200 s): 44% fewer sessions, 10 more turns per session, peak offered load 1.2 vs 2.95 turns/s, in-flight ~6 vs 15-32, and a lighter gap tail. The mean gap is about the same, because Little's law and the L2 size pin it.
The model is in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/ (tiersim.py, design.py; final3.py gives these numbers).
risks: Metastable collapse: queue-time invalidation. If a sustained queue forms after the working set passes L2 (about minute 25), L2 hits that were valid on arrival get evicted while requests wait. They then recompute, which lengthens the queue further. Neither tiered arm is protected; this is the x10/x1 failure. Mitigation: run three_tier_wc first as a pilot. If the waiting queue stays above ~5 for more than 2 min between minutes 20 and 45, abort and move the median to 50 s.

The SSD share is modest: 8-11% of returns (~280-400 restores per arm) against ~19% (840-890) at x70. That is enough for TTFT distributions, but thin for telling three_tier_to from three_tier_wc in the tails. A lower gap sigma (0.6) roughly doubles the share (17-21% in the model at C=80) at the cost of a less realistic, more periodic gap shape.

The SSD phase is transient: about 20-23 minutes (turns ≥ ~30) inside a run of about 65-75 minutes, because the cohort ramps up and then drains. Report by turn index or phase. Whole-run averages dilute the effect about 3x.

hbm_host and hbm_lru will still queue in the late phase. The model predicts mean TTFT of 47-67 s and ~115 s, and run times of about 2.5 h and 4.3 h. Set CLIENT_TIMEOUT to about 9000 s and compare over the common turns. The model was 1.6-2x too pessimistic about collapsed arms against the measured x70 and x10 runs.

Coarse model: the ITL fit comes from 25-35K-token contexts, but late turns reach 45-55K. The model does not separate the timeout and wait_complete prefetch policies. Page-level radix eviction is approximated as per-session LRU with leaf-first partial hits.
Selection bias: only 228 conversations have exactly 50 turns, and all of them are SWE-bench, with no GAIA or WildClaw. The same 72, chosen by seed, are used on every arm.

The gap model is synthetic. The lognormal breaks direct comparability with the x70/x10/x1 GAP-scale series. The gaps must be baked into a derived trace: the client's --gap-sample draws from one shared RNG in completion order, which would give each arm different gaps.

Plumbing: run_compare.sh does not export or record ARRIVAL, so pass ARRIVAL=0.5 in the environment and add it to config.txt. max-running-requests (64) is below C (72), but that is harmless because in-flight stays around 6. The L1 pool, not the running-request cap, limits running requests at late contexts (~16-20).

Realism: the idle-to-active ratio (72 − 6)/6 ≈ 10 is about twice TraceLab's R=5.07 at 1-h retention. The median gap of 40 s sits between TraceLab's mean tool latency (18 s) and its median human think time (84 s), so it models supervised agents or agents with slow tools, not raw SWE-bench tool pacing (0.7 s).
